blocks.title: Introduction
blocks.content:
# Introduction

Health products pass through multiple supply chain partners and processes as they move from manufacturers to end-users. For transactions to be seamless, all stakeholders must consistently identify health products using standardized information.

For example, if a country’s central warehouse receives a shipment of vaccines with identifiers that do not match its standardized data, manual reconciliation will be required. This can lead to delays, errors, and distribution disruptions, ultimately impacting health outcomes.

Uniform and standardized product information builds trust am

summary.text: Introduces product master data and its role in digital health supply chains (Fig. 1–3), alignment with the WHO Digital Implementation Investment Guide (DIIG, Fig. 4), WHO SMART Guidelines L1–L5 knowledge layers and ANC workflow connections (Fig. 5–6), the Digital Health Supply Chain (DHSC) architecture framework (Fig. 7), handbook methodology, target users across Chapters 1–7, and scenarios for using the handbook.

blocks.title: Establishing regulatory policies to promote product master data standardization
blocks.content:
# 01. Establishing regulatory policies to promote product master data standardization

Manufacturers and distributors of health products are the source of truth for product master data. Ensuring that manufacturers and distributors consistently provide product master data in a standardized and uniform format is crucial for enabling interoperability and leveraging automation through barcode scanning.

Regulatory organizations play a key role in establishing policies and legislation that mandate and enforce requirements for manufacturers and distributors to supply standardized product master data

summary.text: Chapter 1 overview explaining the role of Ministries of Health and National Regulatory Authorities (NRAs) in establishing policies and legislation that mandate manufacturers and distributors to supply standardized product master data.

# 02. Instituting data management and governance policies

For effective use of data in operations, analysis, and decision-making, the integrity and quality of data must be consistently and continuously maintained. Establishing data management policies to maintain master data structures, definitions, and operational procedures is crucial for sustaining data integrity and quality. Data management policies should ensure adherence to principles of privacy, security, and ethical data usage. # 03. Deploying appropriate technology to manage product master data

blocks.title: Leveraging the WHO-hosted PCMT
blocks.content:
# 06. Leveraging the WHO-hosted PCMT

Countries planning to implement a digital tool to manage product master data may consider using the WHO–hosted PCMT as an initial option. This tool can serve as a starting point to manage national health product master data while countries build the necessary technical resources and capacity to implement an in-country–hosted solution. Alternatively, countries may continue using the WHO-hosted PCMT if it meets their ongoing needs.

The WHO-hosted PCMT will be available in 2026. Fig. 14 illustrates a conceptual model of how countries can leverage the PCMT to

summary.text: Chapter 6: Describes the WHO-hosted Product Catalogue Management Tool (PCMT) (available in 2026), its conceptual architecture linking the WHO Global Catalogue with Country Catalogues A and B (Fig. 14), and its user-group/category access permission model (`WHOGroup`, `CAGroup`, `CBGroup`), cross-catalogue associations, and copy rules.

blocks.title: Sharing product master data as a global good
blocks.content:
# 07. Sharing product master data as a global good

Sharing health product master data with a global repository—such as the WHO Global Product Catalogue—holds significant value and importance as a global good for several reasons:

- **Access to accurate information:** A centralized repository enables health professionals and organizations worldwide to access accurate and up-to-date information on health products.
- **Standardization:** A global repository aggregates master data from multiple sources for the same or similar products and facilitates the harmonization of data differences to suppo

summary.text: Chapter 7: Explains the value of sharing national product master data as a global good with the WHO Global Product Catalogue (accurate information, standardization, reduced redundancy, crisis management, equal access, capacity building) and presents the bidirectional data-sharing model across countries and the WHO-hosted PCMT (Fig. 15).
